name: RKE2
summary: SUSE’s security-focused Kubernetes distribution: one binary per node, hardened defaults, FIPS-validated crypto and close alignment with upstream.
intro: RKE2 (also called RKE Government) is a Kubernetes distribution from SUSE’s Rancher team. You install a single `rke2` binary and run it as a `server` (control plane plus etcd) or an `agent` (worker). The binary pulls a runtime image with containerd, runc and the kubelet, then writes the API server, scheduler, controller manager and etcd as static Pods that the kubelet supervises. Agents register with a server on port 9345; the Kubernetes API stays on 6443. Embedded etcd is the default datastore, and three servers is the recommended HA setup.

It borrows its installer and supervisor from K3s, Rancher’s lightweight distribution, but stays closer to upstream Kubernetes, and unlike the older RKE1 it doesn’t depend on Docker. The difference is in the defaults: components are compiled with Go’s FIPS 140-2 validated BoringCrypto module, a `profile: cis` setting turns on the Pod Security and network policy controls the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark expects, and every component is scanned for CVEs in the build pipeline. Canal is the default CNI (Cilium, Calico and Flannel are bundled too), and since v1.36 new clusters get Traefik instead of the retired Ingress NGINX.
strengths: Hardened by default: passes most CIS Kubernetes Benchmark controls out of the box, with a published self-assessment for each version
FIPS 140-2 builds and a DISA STIG make it one of the few distributions that US federal and defence buyers can approve as is
Simple operations borrowed from K3s: one binary, one `config.yaml`, a bundled CNI, CoreDNS, metrics-server and ingress, and air-gapped installs from image tarballs
Open source under Apache 2.0, runs standalone or provisioned and upgraded by Rancher
limits: RKE2 won’t change the host OS: CIS kernel parameters and other host-level settings are still your job
Switching the CNI or the cluster and service CIDRs on a running cluster isn’t supported; pick before first start or rebuild
Heavier than K3s: SUSE asks for at least 2 CPUs and 4 GB RAM per server, and 8 GB is recommended
Some extras are paid: SUSE’s Rancher Prime subscription brings up to five years of support per release, and the old Ingress NGINX chart leaves community builds in v1.37

story: Rancher Labs had two Kubernetes distributions by 2019. RKE (now called RKE1) ran every Kubernetes component, including the control plane, as Docker containers, and stayed close to upstream. K3s, released in February 2019, was a single small binary built for edge devices, easy to install but diverging from upstream in places. Rancher’s US federal customers wanted something else again: a distribution they could get through a security accreditation, with FIPS-validated cryptography, SELinux support and CIS-compliant defaults.

Rancher’s answer, first tagged in May 2020 and released as v1.18.9+rke2r1 in October 2020, was RKE2, “also known as RKE Government”. It took K3s’s installer and supervisor process but ran upstream components as static Pods under containerd, with no Docker. SUSE bought Rancher Labs in December 2020; from Rancher 2.6 in 2021, Rancher could provision RKE2 clusters itself, and in November 2022 DISA approved and published an RKE2 STIG.
When RKE1 reached end of life on July 31, 2025, Rancher 2.12 stopped managing RKE1 clusters and told users to move to RKE2. RKE2 is now Rancher’s main datacenter distribution, with K3s for the edge.

choices.choice: Static Pods under containerd instead of Docker containers
choices.why: RKE1 needed Docker on every node to run the control plane. Writing the control plane as static Pod manifests lets the kubelet supervise it like any other Pod, and drops a whole container engine from the node.

choices.choice: Reuse K3s’s supervisor, not its trimmed-down Kubernetes
choices.why: K3s had proved that one binary and one config file made Kubernetes easy to run, but it diverged from upstream to stay small. RKE2 kept the operating model and shipped standard components, which matters when an auditor compares your cluster with upstream benchmarks.
Federal systems must use FIPS 140-2 validated cryptographic modules. Building every Go component against the validated BoringCrypto module meets that without separate patched builds.
